findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: 1,285 council homes (3.4% of stock) currently fail decency standards, including 160 with serious hazards.
findings.detail: As of June 2026, 1,285 properties across the 37,375-home stock fail decency standards (3.4% of stock). Of these, 160 represent Category 1 hazards under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System, defined as posing immediate health and safety risks (0.4% of stock). While the Council notes these proportions are "low," it also acknowledges that fixing them requires "clear, current evidence on condition, performance and risk."
findings.matters: Homes with decency failures and Category 1 hazards create regulatory risk, tenant welfare liability, and ongoing reputational exposure. The absolute numbers indicate significant maintenance obligations competing for resources in a financially constrained HRA.
findings.figures: 1,285 decency failures (3.4%); 160 Category 1 hazards (0.4%)
findings.quote: At the time of writing in June 2026, there were 1,285 total property failures identified across the whole of our 35,375 properties, which accounts for approximately 3.4% of our stock. Of these, 160 relate to Category 1 hazards under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS), representing 0.4% of our stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: 30% of council homes fall below 2030 energy efficiency standards with estimated £641m investment required.
findings.detail: Currently 11,165 homes (30% of stock) are rated EPC D or below, below the minimum standard required by 2030. The Council acknowledges meeting this standard "will require substantial additional investment over the upcoming five years, adding pressure to the HRA." Pilot programmes (150 air source heat pumps, five solar PV schemes 2026–2028) are underway but represent a fraction of total need.
findings.matters: The Council faces legal obligation to upgrade 11,000+ homes by 2030, with non-compliance carrying regulatory penalties. The investment requirement adds materially to the £641m identified gap and likely depends on external grant funding or private investment.
findings.figures: 11,165 homes below EPC C (30% of 37,375 stock); 26,091 homes at C or above (70%)
findings.quote: all housing to a minimum energy efficiency rating of band C by 2030

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: Building safety investment costs remain unknown and uncertain.
findings.detail: The £641m five-year investment assessment is explicitly incomplete on fire and building safety costs. The Council states separately that "the future scale of investment remains uncertain and will continue to affect long-term financial planning and investment decisions." This applies to 25 high-rise buildings undergoing mandatory upgrades and mid-rise blocks currently being assessed for potential future regulatory expansion.
findings.matters: Unknown building safety costs create material financial planning risk. If actual costs exceed current budgeting, the HRA's constrained capacity means additional funding would need to be found through increased debt, further asset sales, or General Fund support.
findings.figures: 25 high-rise buildings in active safety upgrade programmes; mid-rise blocks under assessment; costs unquantified
findings.quote: The future scale of investment remains uncertain and will continue to affect long-term financial planning and investment decisions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: Stock decline will continue despite new-build programme unless Government Right to Buy reforms pass.
findings.detail: The Council targets 1,000 new homes between 2023/24 and 2028/29 but forecasts RTB losses of 1,050 homes in the same period, producing net stock decline. The forecast assumes Government reforms reduce RTB losses from current 400/year to 150/year. If reforms do not pass and current 400/year RTB loss rates persist, cumulative losses would reach 2,000 homes, far exceeding new-build plans and deepening the financial spiral.
findings.matters: A shrinking stock base progressively reduces the HRA's income capacity while fixed costs remain, creating a vicious cycle. Projections depend on Government policy decisions outside the Council's control, creating financial planning uncertainty.
findings.figures: Target 1,000 new builds 2023/24–2028/29; forecast RTB loss 1,050 homes (1,500–2,000 if reforms fail); current loss rate 398/year average
findings.quote: However, if Right to Buy sales continue at around 300 homes a year, this will not be enough to maintain current stock levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: Right to Buy creates £39,000 funding loss per replacement home, draining HRA capital.
findings.detail: The Council has lost an average of 398 homes per year to Right to Buy sales over the past five years. When the Council uses RTB receipts to acquire replacement stock, there is an average shortfall of £39,000 between the sale receipt and the acquisition cost. This creates a net cost to the HRA for each property lost through RTB, simultaneously shrinking the income-generating stock base.
findings.matters: This structural funding gap means RTB sales directly drain capital from the HRA while reducing the rental income stream needed to service maintenance and debt. The dual impact worsens long-term HRA viability and forces either additional borrowing or disposal of other assets to maintain housing provision.
findings.figures: £39,000 average gap per replacement; 398 homes/year average loss; 35,300+ homes lost since 1979
findings.quote: At current values, there is an average £39,000 gap between Right to Buy sale receipts and the cost of buying a replacement property.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 AMS HPC Final September
findings.headline: Council requires £45 million in permanent HRA revenue savings to afford minimum housing maintenance.
findings.detail: The Council's analysis determined that permanent savings of £45m are needed from the HRA revenue budget simply to deliver minimum required housing improvement works, before any investment in stock growth. The document notes this figure is "likely to be a significant underestimate, as some fire and building safety costs remain unknown and it does not account for changes arising from Decent Homes 2 or MEES," indicating unquantified costs could substantially increase this requirement.
findings.matters: A requirement to find £45m in permanent HRA savings indicates a structural imbalance between rental income and maintenance costs. This scale of savings requirement typically requires either major asset disposals, service reductions, or cross-subsidy from the General Fund—each creating financial risk.
findings.figures: £45m permanent savings required; total identified investment need £641,005,032.45 over 5 years
findings.quote: Our analysis suggests we may need around £45m of permanent HRA revenue savings to deliver the minimum required housing improvement works, before setting aside investment for an increased Stock Increase Programme.

However the paper states this position 'depends on delivery of Future Sheffield savings, disciplined budget management, protecting the Council's funding base and avoiding reliance on one-off measures'. Future Sheffield 'remains the Council's primary vehicle for delivering long-term financial sustainability'.
findings.matters: A lender must distinguish between medium-term improvements from baseline funding (structural) versus those dependent on programme delivery (at-risk). This paper makes clear the outlook is conditional on Future Sheffield landing.
findings.figures: MTFS covers 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.quote: The Council's medium-term outlook is stronger than in recent years, but this depends on delivery of Future Sheffield savings, disciplined budget management, protecting the Council's funding base and avoiding reliance on one-off measures to fund recurring cost pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Overall forecast overspend has fallen dramatically from peaks exceeding £30m in 2025/26 to £8.35m at Q1 2026/27, indicating significant financial recovery underway.
findings.detail: The paper notes 'a significant improvement compared with the position experienced during 2025/26, with forecast overspends reducing from peaks in excess of £30m to £8.4m'. This reflects both a stronger Local Government Finance Settlement and progress on financial discipline and transformation. The council states this demonstrates 'a Council that is in a stronger financial position than in recent years'.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors evaluate trajectory alongside current position. A council moving from crisis overspends to managed pressures demonstrates financial control and improving creditworthiness. However, the improvement remains conditional on continued delivery.
findings.figures: £30m+ overspends in 2025/26, £8.35m forecast overspend at Q1 2026/27
findings.quote: The trend chart shows a significant improvement compared with the position experienced during 2025/26, with forecast overspends reducing from peaks in excess of £30m to £8.4m at Quarter 1 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - Housing Committee
findings.headline: A one-off £2.29m release of corporate housing contingency reserves is reducing the reported overspend but explicitly does not address the underlying exempt accommodation subsidy problem.
findings.detail: The corporate position shows a £2.29m favourable variance due to release of a housing-related contingency. The paper makes clear this 'should be recognised that this is a one-off corporate mitigation rather than a permanent solution to the underlying subsidy issue'. This signals the council is using reserves to offset a recurring structural pressure while seeking a policy solution.
findings.matters: Using one-off reserves to fund recurring costs is unsustainable and signals the reported position depends on either delivering savings, securing policy change, or drawing reserves further. It indicates reserves are being used for time-buying rather than transformation.
findings.figures: £2.29m corporate favourable position
findings.quote: Whilst this improves the in-year forecast, it should be recognised that this is a one-off corporate mitigation rather than a permanent solution to the underlying subsidy issue.

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Supported exempt accommodation creates a £2.3m structural financial pressure: the difference between Housing Benefit the council pays out and the level of central government subsidy received.
findings.detail: Within Strategic and Enabling Services' £2.09m overspend, exempt accommodation accounts for £2.3m and is described as 'a structural financial challenge' and 'a national issue'. The paper states: the mismatch arises because 'Housing Benefit paid out by local authorities' exceeds 'the level of subsidy received from central government'. Various organisations have called for changes to regulations to address this, but 'further dialogue between local and central government is needed'. This pressure was consistent in 2025/26 and continues.
findings.matters: Unlike savings delays, this hole cannot be closed through council management action alone. It signals either a permanent cost or a bet on central government policy change—neither of which Sheffield can control.
findings.figures: £2.3m exempt accommodation pressure within £2.09m Strategic and Enabling Services overspend
findings.quote: the mismatch between Housing Benefit paid out by local authorities and the level of subsidy received from central government is a national issue. Changes to the relevant regulations that removes or reduces the financial burden imposed on local authorities has been called for by various organisations.

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - Housing Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care's £5.33m overspend is driven by delays in transformation benefits (£2.6m) and prior-year savings carryover (£4.5m), not by demand exceeding the investment made in this year's budget.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget included additional investment to address known demographic and demand pressures in Adult Social Care. The current overspend reflects slower-than-planned delivery of Future Sheffield benefits and carryover of undelivered 2025/26 savings. The council states this 'should be viewed primarily as a delivery challenge rather than evidence of significant deterioration in underlying demand'. Employee forecasts show a favourable £1.9m, as hiring for transformation capacity remains in progress.
findings.matters: This distinguishes between a temporary funding gap (when transformation lands) and a structural demand problem (requiring service cuts). The paper indicates the former, but it depends on acceleration of Future Sheffield delivery.
findings.figures: £5.33m overspend, £2.6m Future Sheffield slippage, £4.5m prior-year carryover, £1.9m employee budget favourable
findings.quote: The pressure is mainly within purchasing budgets and is driven by savings from 2025/26 (c.£4.5m) and 2026/27 taking longer to deliver than planned, including Future Sheffield savings (£2.6m)

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - Housing Committee
findings.headline: The £8.35m General Fund overspend is composed largely of £7.93m in delayed savings delivery rather than underlying service demand exceeding budget.
findings.detail: Of the £21.37m in savings targets for 2026/27, the council is forecasting only £13.42m delivery by year-end, creating a £7.93m shortfall. The largest gaps are in Future Sheffield programmes (£4.15m) and prior-year Adult Social Care savings (£3.80m). The council describes this as 'a delivery challenge rather than evidence of significant deterioration in underlying demand', distinguishing a temporary implementation timing issue from structural demand growth.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether an overspend will reverse when transformation benefits land, or whether it signals persistent structural pressure. This paper indicates the former—but only if Future Sheffield delivery accelerates.
findings.figures: £8.35m overspend, £7.93m savings shortfall, £21.37m budgeted savings, £13.42m forecast delivery
findings.quote: A key feature of the Quarter 1 position is that most of the reported pressure is linked to savings delivery risk rather than a large underlying service overspend. The forecast identifies £7.93m of under-delivering 2026/27 Savings Plans

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Investment income declining as interest rates normalize and cash balances fall
findings.detail: Investment returns are averaging 4.05–4.10% in 2026/27, down from 5.19–5.32% in 2025/26. Investment balances stood at £253m at end Q1 and are expected to fall over the financial year as capital expenditure proceeds. While income is forecast to remain 'in line with budget,' absolute returns are declining as rates fall from their recent peak.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Interest rate environment remains uncertain and elevated, creating ongoing refinancing risk
findings.detail: PWLB rates have risen to levels unseen for 25 years, with the 10-year rate at 5.55% at end June 26. Rates have continued to rise since, driven by market concerns about the US-Iran conflict and elevated inflation risks. The UK base rate is expected to be cut only gradually, and there remains 'significant uncertainty in gilt markets.' This environment underpins the council's decision to delay borrowing but creates material risk if rates remain stuck at these levels.
findings.matters: Elevated and uncertain rates drive the council's entire treasury strategy and directly threaten to increase the cost of servicing debt. Geopolitical risk adds asymmetric upside to rate forecasts
findings.figures: PWLB 10-year rate 5.55% at end June 26; rates have increased since; 25-year high context
findings.quote: PWLB 10 year was at 5.55% at the end of June 26 and has only increased since as markets view global economic risks and inflation risks to be higher due to the ongoing conflict between USA and Iran.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Treasury management budget balanced and on track despite challenging interest rate environment
findings.detail: The treasury budget is forecast with zero variance: investment income £8.1m, borrowing costs £24.55m, and MRP £14.25m all tracking to budget. General Fund financing costs as a proportion of revenue are expected to fall to 15.9% from the budgeted 16.8%—an improvement driven by the lower borrowing forecast. This demonstrates the council is maintaining cost control despite high external rates.
findings.matters: A lender cares whether the council is forecasting to budget and whether financing costs are under control. Better-than-budget outturn on a major spending area is a positive indicator in a high-rate environment
findings.figures: Treasury budget variance £0.01m; GF financing costs forecast 15.9% vs 16.8% budget (vs 16.6% actual 2025/26); HRA financing costs 5.3% vs 6.9% budget
findings.quote: No new borrowing has been taken in line with forecast which didn't include additional cost until the second half of the year.

findings.detail: Disposals from the Heart of the City development are now expected to be delayed 'until more favourable economic conditions' allow the council to maximize proceeds. Assets will be held and financed for an extended period, meaning interest charges and Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) will continue 'higher for longer' than originally planned, though offset by rental income. This effectively extends the debt maturity and delays planned disposal proceeds.
findings.matters: This extends the council's debt profile, locks in higher annual financing costs, and delays proceeds that may have been intended for other priorities or to reduce debt
findings.figures: Delay quantum not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: Anticipated disposals of Blocks in the Heart of the City development are now expected to be delayed until more favourable economic conditions help maximise the benefit of the disposal. As a result, assets will be held and financed for longer, meaning the cost of interest and the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charged to revenue will be higher for longer

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: HRA capital programme significantly underspending (£32m or 27% below budget)
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account capital expenditure is now forecast at £83.3m against a budget of £115.0m—a variance of £31.6m. The HRA is forecasting a substantially lower capital investment programme over the next two years, with borrowing requirements reduced by approximately £50m. This represents a major scale-back from planned housing investment.
findings.matters: A 27% shortfall in capital spend signals either delivery challenges or significant rescoping of housing investment priorities, both material to lenders' assessment of the council's execution capability and credibility
findings.figures: HRA capex forecast £83.3m vs budget £115.0m (variance £31.6m); borrowing requirement reduced by around £50m over next 2 years

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: LOBO loans at elevated risk of being called, forcing immediate refinancing at current high rates
findings.detail: The council explicitly flags 'material risk' that Lender Option Borrower Option loans will be called. These loans remain 'at elevated risk of being called' and would be repaid at par to de-risk the portfolio. Early repayment would force new borrowing sooner than planned, removing the council's ability to wait for lower rates and reducing financial flexibility.

findings.figures: Specific LOBO loan amounts not separately itemized in this paper

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - 2627 Q1 Treasury Management Report
findings.headline: Borrowing forecast slashed by £120m due to high interest rates and geopolitical uncertainty
findings.detail: The council originally budgeted to take £180m of new external borrowing in 2026/27 but now forecasts only £60m. Strong cash balances have allowed it to delay borrowing while rates remain elevated around 5% and volatile due to the US-Iran conflict. The finance team estimates that if the full budget had been externalized at current rates, the additional annual cost would be roughly £9m.
findings.matters: This is a major swing from plan. It indicates a strong balance sheet but also material interest rate risk and potential for capital programme deferrals if cash runs down faster than expected
findings.figures: £180m budgeted borrowing vs £60m forecast; interest rates approximately 5%; potential additional cost £9m if full budget externalized
findings.quote: If 100% of 26/27 forecast for activity financed by borrowing was externalised at current interest rates of around 5%, this would see an additional (fully year cost) of around £9m.

findings.paper_title: AH Land Disposals (Phase 1) - Form 2 - FPPC 21-09-2026 v3_00 FINAL
findings.headline: Disposal agreements conditional on Registered Providers securing Homes England grant funding; council sacrificing capital receipts for uncertain delivery
findings.detail: Each Registered Provider has indicated they expect to secure Homes England Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) funding. Disposal agreements include conditionality requiring planning permission and third-party grant funding to be secured within agreed timeframes (typically 2 years), with anticipated completion 2028/29. The council is reducing its current capital position based on the assumption that these external funders will provide grants that individual Registered Providers must secure through competitive bidding.
findings.matters: The council is reducing its current capital position as an investment in housing delivery that is dependent on securing external grant funding outside its direct control. If Homes England or SYMCA funding does not materialise for any sites, the council will have sacrificed capital receipts without achieving the intended housing outcome.
findings.figures: c.200 affordable homes targeted; typically 2-year funding/planning window; majority completion anticipated 2028/29; SYMCA has secured £118m from National Housing Development Fund from April 2026
findings.quote: Any contract for disposal will be conditional on securing planning and grant funding.

findings.paper_title: AH Land Disposals (Phase 1) - Form 2 - FPPC 21-09-2026 v3_00 FINAL
findings.headline: Council deliberately accepting below-market bids for all seven sites to deliver housing; capital receipts sacrificed for policy outcome
findings.detail: All seven sites have received bids from Registered Providers at valuations below market value (all except one HRA site). The council acknowledges this represents a deliberate choice to accept lower valuations to secure 100% affordable housing delivery (c.200 homes at social rent) rather than maximize capital receipts through market sale, which would deliver only approximately 13 affordable homes under current planning policy. This sacrifice of capital income will reduce funding available for other priorities including the Accommodation Strategy and corporate maintenance backlog. The financial amounts are contained in the restricted appendix.
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate councils' capital resources and financial flexibility. A deliberate strategy to reduce capital receipts materially affects the council's capacity to invest in priorities including asset maintenance, which lenders monitor closely.
findings.figures: c.200 affordable homes at social rent; approximately 13 affordable homes under current planning policy if land sold at market value
findings.quote: The decision therefore represents a positive and deliberate choice to use the value of these assets to support the delivery of affordable housing in the city, rather than to potentially maximise capital receipts for investment in other corporate priorities.

Identified risks include taxbase growth slowdown or collection rate weakness during the remainder of the year.
findings.matters: Large-scale Collection Fund volatility creates uncertainty around a material portion of the council's income base, making budget forecasts less reliable.
findings.figures: Collection Fund scale £454.9m; position dependent on collection rates, appeals and taxbase assumptions
findings.quote: Given the scale of the Collection Fund, relatively small changes in underlying assumptions can materially affect the final outturn. The position will continue to be monitored closely throughout the year.

findings.detail: Recent Valuation Office decisions enabled the council to release provisions previously established to cover appeals, creating a favourable variance on Business Rates. This is a one-off benefit from reassessment of appeals provisions; the underlying collection position remains on budget.
findings.matters: When favorable outcomes are driven by provision releases rather than improved collection performance, the underlying budget position is weaker than headline figures suggest, reducing forecast reliability.

This reflects improved Local Government Finance Settlement and Future Sheffield planning assumptions. However, council makes clear this progress 'remains dependent on successful delivery of transformation activity and savings plans throughout the year'. Positive direction but not yet stable.

However, fragility of the improvement (dependent on single transformation programme with early slippage) should not be overlooked.

External residential placements experiencing cost and demand pressures. Numbers of children entering care remain comparatively low, reflecting prevention programmes, but cost volatility persists.
findings.matters: Council's own assessment ranks this as a top financial risk despite small current variance. Placement costs are high-value transactions; demand can spike unpredictably. For a lender, this is a tail risk that needs monitoring even when current position is favorable.

findings.detail: Corporate position shows £2.29m favorable variance, mainly from 'release of a corporate housing contingency established to manage risks associated with supported exempt accommodation'. Council explicitly notes this is 'a one-off corporate mitigation rather than a permanent solution to the underlying subsidy issue'. Council warned in its opening statement that medium-term outlook 'depends on... avoiding reliance on one-off measures to fund recurring cost pressures'.
findings.matters: Using reserves to bridge a recurring subsidy gap (£2.3m exempt accommodation pressure offset by contingency release) is defensive deployment of reserves rather than strategic. This pattern reduces reserve adequacy if structural pressures persist or expand.

findings.headline: Supported exempt accommodation creates £2.3m recurring subsidy gap, characterized as 'structural financial challenge' requiring government policy change
findings.detail: Housing Benefit shows £2.3m pressure from mismatch between Housing Benefit paid by council and subsidy received from government for supported exempt accommodation. This pressure was consistent in 2025/26 and continues. Council describes this as a national issue and calls for changes to relevant regulations, indicating this cannot be solved by local action and will persist until policy changes.

findings.detail: Council identifies Future Sheffield as its 'primary vehicle for delivering long-term financial sustainability' and has built its budget on assumed savings from this programme. Q1 forecast shows £7.9m under-delivery, characterized by council as 'timing and implementation of transformation activity'. Council repeatedly states the medium-term financial outlook depends on successful delivery of this programme throughout the year.
findings.matters: The council's financial strategy is heavily weighted to this single transformation programme. Recruitment is under way but the paper warns that further delays or turnover could push most benefits into 2027/28, creating risk that the council is trading short-term financial relief for long-term delivery risk.
findings.matters: Using vacancies to manage budget while these same vacancies impede delivery of planned savings creates a vicious cycle where the council cannot catch up to its improvement trajectory.
findings.figures: £1.9m staffing underspend; potential push of benefits to 2027/28 if recruitment delayed
findings.quote: Vacancies are slowing delivery, despite £1.9m of lower staffing costs. Recruitment is under way, but delays or further turnover could push most benefits into 2027/28.

findings.matters: Concurrent shortfalls in multiple income sources indicate systemic income forecasting or collection weakness that may recur and limits the council's ability to balance budgets through income growth.

findings.matters: This is a structural income shortfall outside the council's direct control that requires provision from central funds and represents an ongoing claim on council reserves or alternative resources.

findings.matters: Multi-year savings shortfalls compound budget pressure and indicate some planned improvements are not materialising, reducing the council's flexibility to manage future pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 – 2627 Q1 Detailed Committee Budget Monitoring
findings.headline: Children's Services placement budgets under pressure despite £13.6m budget increase in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has increased Children's Services placement budgets by £13.6m but demand continues to outpace funding. findings.matters: Persistent placement cost pressures despite significant budget increases suggest demand is structural and may create ongoing pressure on council budgets or require further investment.

findings.matters: The council's major transformation programme is not delivering expected financial benefits on schedule, suggesting delays to anticipated improvements in operational efficiency and service delivery.

findings.quote: The DSG overspend of £29m is unlikely to be resolved without additional funding and increased SEN costs and number of places continue to create pressures.

findings.quote: Time-limited transport grants remain at risk if programme delivery milestones are not achieved.

findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is currently forecast as balanced, but repairs and maintenance carry acknowledged cost pressures. findings.matters: Damp and mould management in council housing implies either building condition issues that require remediation expenditure, or ongoing costs that may not be adequately budgeted. findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - AHSC Committee
findings.headline: Medium-term financial sustainability is explicitly stated to depend on delivery of Future Sheffield transformation, with strategy relying on avoiding one-off mitigations for recurring pressures
findings.detail: The council's updated Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) is described as showing 'a significantly stronger financial outlook' but with clear caveats: that position 'depends on delivering transformation, maintaining financial discipline, protecting the funding base and avoiding reliance on one-off measures'. The paper emphasises multiple times that Future Sheffield is 'the Council's primary vehicle' for long-term sustainability and 'fundamental to maintaining a balanced and sustainable financial position over the medium term'.
findings.matters: A lender is exposed to execution risk if the medium-term plan depends critically on a transformation programme that is already slipping (£4.15m in Q1). The paper also signals reliance on one-off corporate mitigations (contingency releases) rather than structural solutions, which is unsustainable.
findings.figures: Future Sheffield savings target: £17.57m total; Q1 slippage: £4.15m
findings.quote: The Council set a balanced 2026/27 budget and has a significantly stronger medium-term outlook than in recent years, but that position depends on delivering transformation, maintaining financial discipline, protecting the funding base and avoiding reliance on one-off measures to fund recurring cost pressures... Future Sheffield remains the Council's primary vehicle for delivering long-term financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 2627 Q1 Budget Monitoring Report - AHSC Committee

findings.detail: Although external residential placements are currently showing only a £0.86m overspend against the directorate budget, the paper flags placement demand as volatile and the council's primary financial risk in this service. The council has invested to better align budgets with demand, but demand management through prevention and early intervention is ongoing and outcomes remain uncertain.
findings.matters: A lender sees placement demand volatility as a risk that could swing a service from apparently controlled to significantly overspent within a quarter. The council's ability to manage this through prevention is unproven, and placement costs are market-driven and outside the council's control.

findings.detail: A £2.3m pressure within Housing Benefit arises from the mismatch between what Sheffield pays in Housing Benefit for exempt accommodation and what central government reimburses. The paper explicitly states this 'continues to represent a structural financial challenge' and was 'consistent in 2025/26'. It is being partially mitigated by a corporate contingency release of £2.29m, which the paper notes is 'a one-off corporate mitigation rather than a permanent solution to the underlying subsidy issue'.

It indicates fiscal vulnerability to national policy decisions about Housing Benefit subsidy rates, and reliance on contingency reserves rather than resolving the underlying issue.

findings.quote: The mismatch between Housing Benefit paid out by local authorities and the level of subsidy received from central government is a national issue... This pressure was consistent in 2025/26 and this issue continues to represent a structural financial challenge... this is a one-off corporate mitigation rather than a permanent solution to the underlying subsidy issue.

findings.quote: During 2025/26, work has continued to develop the programme and align it more closely with financial planning. While early benefits are beginning to emerge, the majority of financial impact is expected in future years. Delivery of the programme therefore remains critical to achieving a sustainable financial position over the medium term.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) pressures in high needs continuing outside General Fund but remain material financial risk
findings.detail: DSG pressures, particularly high needs expenditure, sit outside the General Fund position reported here but are flagged as 'a significant financial risk' requiring 'separate statutory accounting arrangements and recovery planning'. This is an additional liabilities layer not captured in the £11.1m headline overspend.
findings.matters: DSG deficits can accumulate as statutory duties that councils cannot avoid. Though accounted separately, high needs spending often spills into General Fund eventually, creating hidden future liabilities.
findings.figures: DSG pressures (amount not disclosed in this report)
findings.quote: The Council continues to manage pressures within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), particularly in relation to high needs expenditure. While these pressures sit outside the General Fund position reported above, they remain a significant financial risk and are subject to separate statutory accounting arrangements and recovery planning.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Housing structural deficit: £2.9m subsidy gap between cost and Housing Benefit recovery
findings.detail: Supported exempt accommodation creates a structural gap between costs incurred and government subsidy recovered. Council describes this as 'a structural financial challenge' and notes it 'has remained consistent throughout the year'. Work to reduce via partnership arrangements and appeals is underway but 'remains a complex area with a degree of uncertainty around the extent and timing of financial benefit.'
findings.matters: This is a structural mismatch between costs and income that cannot be solved by the council alone; it depends on government subsidy rules and the accuracy of provider claims. It is not a discretionary overspend but a policy-driven deficit.
findings.figures: Supported exempt accommodation £2.9m pressure in Housing Benefit
findings.quote: Supported exempt accommodation (£2.9m pressure in Housing Benefit) This pressure sits within Strategic & Enabling Services budgets and reflects the gap between Housing Benefit paid and the amount reimbursed by government for supported accommodation. This pressure has remained consistent throughout the year and continues to represent a structural financial challenge.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Children's placements £9m overspend with unresolved reliance on high-cost external provision
findings.detail: Placements (residential and independent) are £9m over budget with continued demand for complex needs. Recovery actions focus on expanding in-house provision but progress is slow; council states it is 'expanding in-house fostering and residential provision' but placements remain the largest single pressure within Children's Services (£12.1m total overspend).
findings.matters: Children's placements are high-cost per case and volatile; inability to reduce external placements suggests either insufficient in-house capacity or difficulty managing demand, both indicating future cost pressures.
findings.figures: Placements £9.0m overspend; total Children's Services £12.1m overspend; rising demand for residential and independent settings
findings.quote: Placements (£9.0m overspend) – continued demand for care, with more children placed in higher-cost residential and independent settings

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Reserves being drawn down unsustainably to cover structural deficits; £11.1m overspend funded from reserves
findings.detail: Council explicitly states 'This is not a sustainable approach' yet has depleted reserves significantly over recent years and will use them again in 2025/26. Remaining reserves are 'an important part of the Council's financial resilience and must be protected', creating tension with ongoing deficits that require covering.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover revenue overspends indicates the council cannot live within its income. Reserves are one-time sources; exhausting them leaves the council with no buffer for demand shocks or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £11.1m funded from reserves in 2025/26; ongoing reserves depletion; 2024/25 overspend £34.7m, 2023/24 £15.6m
findings.quote: The Council has made significant use of reserves in recent years to manage financial pressures, resulting in a reduction in available balances. The 2025/26 overspend of £11.1m will be funded from reserves, reflecting the continued use of reserves to manage in-year pressures. This is not a sustainable approach.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: £11.1m overspend masked by one-off corporate actions; underlying demand pressures unchanged
findings.detail: The improved headline position (£7.8m better than Q3) came from £13m contingencies release, £9.8m Collection Fund surplus, £3m treasury benefits, and £3.7m vacancy factor savings — none structural. Council acknowledges: 'the improved position is largely due to one-off corporate actions and year-end adjustments, rather than a reduction in demand for services.'
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether financial improvement is structural or temporary. One-off measures do not solve recurring problems and cannot be relied upon going forward.
findings.figures: £11.1m overspend vs £18.9m Q3 forecast; £13m contingencies; £9.8m Collection Fund surplus; £3m treasury/financing benefits; £3.7m vacancy factor
findings.quote: However, the improved position is largely due to one-off corporate actions and year-end adjustments, rather than a reduction in demand for services. The main drivers of pressure, particularly in social care, SEND and housing, remain in place at year end.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Savings programme delivering only 77% of planned £58.5m target, with £4.5m assessed as permanently undeliverable
findings.detail: Of £13.4m shortfall, £8.9m slipped to next year but £4.5m is undeliverable in-year and requires replacement savings or ongoing budget absorption. Adults' Services particularly weak at 56% delivery. Slippage concentrated in transformation programmes and demand-led services where delivery is proving harder than planned.
findings.matters: A 77% savings delivery rate indicates budget plans rely on actions the council cannot execute reliably. Undeliverable savings must be replaced elsewhere or leave an ongoing structural deficit.
findings.figures: £58.5m planned; £45.1m delivered; £13.4m shortfall; £4.5m undeliverable; Adults 56% delivery vs Neighbourhood Services 98%
findings.quote: The approved 2025/26 budget included £58.5m of savings, of which £45.1m has been delivered in-year, resulting in a shortfall of £13.4m (c.23%). This represents a delivery rate of around 77%, which is lower than in previous years. Of the £13.4m shortfall: around £8.9m relates to slippage into 2026/27, where savings are expected to be delivered later than planned; and around £4.5m is currently assessed as undeliverable in-year, requiring either replacement savings or funding through ongoing budget management.

findings.committee: Adult Health and Social Care Policy Committee
findings.paper_title: 2526 Q4 Budget Monitoring Report - ASC Committee
findings.headline: Adult Social Care £30m overspend driven by uncontrolled demand growth and complex care packages
findings.detail: The largest service pressure (£30m) remains structural: more people requiring support and increasingly complex, expensive care. Some progress on package reviews and stabilisation of costs per case, but overall demand continues rising and planned savings have not delivered in-year, deferring £10.8m (44%) of savings to next year.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically 20-25% of council spending; persistent growth above budget threatens financial sustainability and requires either revenue growth or demand reduction neither of which is assured.
findings.figures: £30.0m overspend; Adults' Services delivered only 56% of planned savings (£10.8m shortfall)
findings.quote: The largest pressure remains within Adults' Social Care. The overspend is mainly due to the cost of care packages, with more people needing support and, increasingly complex and expensive care. Some progress has been made during the year to review and manage packages, and there are early signs that costs per package may be stabilising. However, overall demand continues to rise, and a number of planned savings have not been delivered within the year and are now expected to be delivered next year, meaning the underlying pressure remains.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Complaints handling satisfaction fell to 33.2% (lowest measure) and Stage 1 response time performance is below sector average at 52%
findings.detail: Satisfaction with complaints handling declined year-on-year and is the only perception measure to worsen in 2025/26. Stage 1 responses within timescale are only 52% (target 85%). This is the single worst-performing TSM and a direct outcome of increased demand and capacity pressures. The council acknowledges this is a national trend but remains a regulatory concern.
findings.matters: Poor complaints handling is a regulator priority under the Transparency, Influence and Accountability Standard. Combined with the C3 grade, persistent complaints handling failure could trigger enforcement action. Large repair-related complaint volumes suggest service quality issues are not being resolved quickly.
findings.figures: Satisfaction 33.2% (2025/26, down from 33.8%); Stage 1 responses within timescale 52% (target 85%); Stage 2 responses improved to 22% within timescale (from baseline)
findings.quote: satisfaction with complaints handling remains comparatively low and was the only perception measure that returned a poorer performance in 2025/26 compared to 2024/25, albeit a very small drop from 33.8% to 33.2%. The handling of complaints remains a key area for improvement, both with respect to the speed of response and the way that they are being dealt with.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: New damp and mould reports surged 44% to 2,536 cases in Q4, signalling either worsening stock condition or rising tenant reporting
findings.detail: Pre-Awaab's Law damp and mould cases increased sharply in Q4 (2,536 new cases vs. 1,756 in Q3). While overdue cases fell and the council attributes this to improved reporting and confidence, the volume surge creates service capacity risk. Awaab's Law (September 2023) requires emergency hazards remedied within fixed timeframes; non-compliance exposes tenants to legal claims.
findings.matters: Damp and mould under Awaab's Law carries strict compliance timelines and tenant compensation risk if remediation fails. A 44% case surge suggests either deteriorating stock quality or a backlog of unreported issues now surfacing. Either scenario creates operational and financial risk.
findings.figures: 2,536 new damp/mould cases in Q4 2025/26 (vs. 1,756 in Q3); 133 open cases; 92 overdue cases
findings.quote: New reported cases have increased notably, with 2,536 cases raised in Quarter 4 compared to 1,756 in Quarter 3. This reflects improved reporting, stronger internal recording mechanisms, better identification of issues, and increased resident confidence in coming forward. It also reinforces the need to sustain capacity and maintain momentum in case resolution.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Overdue repairs backlog surged to 8,772 in Q4 2025/26, directly degrading tenant satisfaction and operational capacity
findings.detail: Overdue repairs rose significantly in Q4 after sustained improvements. The backlog now totals 8,772 cases (though down from ~23,000 in January 2024). This directly impacted tenant satisfaction with repairs (down 3% in Q4 despite annual improvement). The council has deployed additional managerial and operational resource but this signals ongoing demand-supply imbalance.
findings.matters: Persistent repairs backlog signals service quality risk and operational stress. Tenant satisfaction declining in Q4 despite annual improvement suggests the service is under pressure. Legal disrepair cases (471 open) create liability exposure.
findings.figures: 8,772 overdue repairs at Q4 2025/26; 16,000 repairs in-progress (down from ~36,000 in Jan 2024); 471 open legal disrepair cases; tenant satisfaction with time to repair fell 3% to 72% in Q4
findings.quote: A key contributing factor is the increase in overdue repairs, which rose to 8,772 in Quarter 4. This growing backlog likely impacted tenant experience during this period and constrained the service's ability to complete repairs within target timescales, contributing to the observed decline in satisfaction over the last quarter.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Electrical safety compliance deadline of 1 November 2026 creates operational and regulatory urgency, with 698 properties still non-compliant
findings.detail: All council homes must hold valid Electrical Installation Condition Reports (EICR) within a five-year compliance cycle by 1 November 2026. As of Q4, 698 properties (just under 2%) remain non-compliant for over 10 years. The council plans to deliver ~1,000 EICR inspections per month through November 2026 to meet the deadline, but this is a significant acceleration from current throughput.
findings.matters: Failure to meet this statutory deadline could result in regulator action and legal liability. The scale of activity required (1,000 inspections/month) signals capacity risk if contractors cannot deliver.
findings.figures: 698 properties non-compliant as of Q4 2025/26 (down from 758 in Q3); compliance deadline 1 November 2026; target delivery ~1,000 inspections/month
findings.quote: Under revised regulations, all properties must be compliant by 1 November 2026, and the Council is working closely with its two principal contractors to increase delivery capacity accordingly.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: C3 regulatory grade (July 2024) means serious failings the council's current arrangements are not strong enough to fix
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grade in July 2024, the second-worst rating, indicating serious failings in delivering Consumer Standards outcomes. The regulator has not yet deployed enforcement powers but confirmed they will keep this under review. The council is required to develop and deliver a significant change plan.
findings.matters: A C3 grade signals potential for regulator intervention (Performance Improvement Plans, Enforcement Notices, or Management Transfer). This is governance and reputational risk for a borrower, and the regulator specifically stated enforcement powers remain available.
findings.figures: C3 grade (on scale C1–C4, where C1 is compliant and C4 is worst); effective from 9 July 2024
findings.quote: The C3 grade means that there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the Consumer Standards, which the landlord's current arrangements are not strong enough to put right. This will be significantly impacting on service outcomes for tenants and/or accountability to tenants.

findings.paper_title: Housing Performance Report (Quarter 4 202526) and Tenant Satisfaction Measures (TSMs) Submission to the Regulator of Social Housing
findings.headline: Rent arrears increased to £10.1m in Q4, up £350k from Q3, driven by housing management system failures
findings.detail: Current tenant rent arrears rose significantly during Q4 2025/26, with the increase directly attributed to problems with the new housing management system implemented in Q3. Automated processes, system-generated letters, and direct debits all failed, forcing staff onto manual work the team could not sustain. This directly impacts Housing Revenue Account income.
findings.matters: Growing rent arrears reduce the HRA's ability to service debt and fund housing operations. System-driven failures create operational risk and suggest capacity pressures in service delivery.
findings.figures: £10.1m current tenant arrears (Q4 2025/26), up £350k from Q3; £4.34m former tenant arrears
findings.quote: The introduction of the new housing management system in Quarter 3 has impacted rent collection performance. Issues with automated processes, inability to send system generated letters and direct debits not working correctly have all created additional manual work that the team has struggled to maintain.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: EWI2 contractor replaced following unsatisfactory performance; delayed completion to Q3 2026/27
findings.detail: Original contractor on external wall insulation phase 2 underperformed and was replaced. New contractor now tasked with 91 properties, target completion Q3 2026/27. Indicates prior procurement/contract management failure and adds further delay to fire safety remedial programme.
findings.matters: Contractor failure affects schedule, cost control, and programme confidence; replacement adds delay to critical remedial work.
findings.figures: 91 remaining properties; target completion Q3 2026/27
findings.quote: The external wall insulation phase 2 (EWI 2 Airey repair and insulation) has a new contractor appointed following the unsatisfactory performance of the original contractor.

findings.headline: Grant-funded energy efficiency programme underperforming against funding conditions; funder notified of clawback risk
findings.detail: 'Delivery to date is lower than originally profiled' on SHDF3 energy efficiency (grant-funded). 'Funder has been kept informed, as the final grant position may be influenced by overall programme delivery across local authorities.' Risk of grant clawback or reduced future allocations if target expenditure not met.
findings.matters: Grant clawback directly reduces HRA resources; also signals delivery risk that could affect future grant eligibility or borrowing capacity from government schemes.

findings.quote: This project is funded by a grant, and in accordance with the conditions of the grant, a certain level of expenditure must be met during year 25/26. Delivery to date is lower than originally profiled, resulting in a variance against budget. The funder has been kept informed, as the final grant position may be influenced by overall programme delivery across local authorities.

findings.paper_title: Form 2 Housing Policy Committee Report Capital Programme 2025-26 Quarter 4 Position - June 2026 V2.0RLGB
findings.headline: Strategic acquisitions for temporary accommodation delayed by structural issues under negotiation with seller
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation acquisitions programme underspent £5.4m (largest single variance) due to 'ongoing negotiations with the seller on structural issues'. Completion pushed from early 2026 to April/May 2026. Suggests due diligence identified defects requiring negotiation on price/remediation.
findings.matters: Structural defects increase lifetime maintenance costs and affect asset quality; negotiations suggest final cost/liability may not yet be settled; impacts HRA long-term asset base.
findings.figures: £5.4m underspend; completion delayed ~3 months

findings.headline: Building Control sign-off delays stalling external wall insulation remedial programme on fire-risk stock
findings.detail: EWI2 (external wall insulation on Airey properties, which carry known fire risk) has £1.59m underspend due to 'delays in obtaining footings/foundations sign-off from Building Control'. 15 properties scheduled for completion by March 2026 were not completed. Programme now expected to finish Q3 2026/27.
findings.matters: Building Control delays on remedial work to known fire-risk housing expose the council to regulatory and legal risk; suggests process bottlenecks beyond the council's control but affecting safety compliance.

findings.quote: This was due in part to delays in obtaining footings/ foundations sign-off from Building Control, which impacted progress on site.
